blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A director must pick which of twelve feeder upgrades go ahead this year. The budget is fixed and each upgrade's cost and value are known. What should the model's variables be?

options.text: Whether each upgrade ranks in the top half, since planners sort by value
options.says: A ranking answers which upgrade is best alone; the question is which combination is best.

options.text: The value of each upgrade, since the model maximizes total value
options.says: The values are known data. The model chooses what to fund, and the value follows.

options.text: Whether each upgrade is approved, since that is what the team decides
options.says: Right: the costs, values and budget are data; the yes/no choice per upgrade is the decision.

options.text: The budget for the year, since the budget limits every plan
options.says: The budget is fixed here, so it is data, not something the model chooses.

origin.section: A Model Starts From the Decisions You Control, One Variable per Choice

questions.stem: Project R7 relocates a line. Project R8 adds a relay that only works on the relocated line. R7 may go ahead without R8. With binaries x_R7 and x_R8, which constraint states the rule?

options.text: x_R8 <= x_R7, since R8 can be funded only together with R7
options.says: Right: R8 can be 1 only when R7 is 1, and R7 alone stays allowed.

options.text: x_R7 <= x_R8, since R7 can be funded only together with R8
options.says: This forbids R7 alone, which the rule allows, and permits R8 alone, which it forbids.

options.text: x_R8 = x_R7, since R8 and R7 can be funded only together
options.says: An equation makes them all-or-nothing, so R7 could no longer go ahead alone.

options.text: x_R7 + x_R8 <= 1, since R7 and R8 can never be funded together
options.says: That is the alternatives rule; it forbids funding both, which is exactly what R8 needs.

origin.section: Constraints Decide Which Plans Are Allowed, and Business Rules Are Constraints Too

questions.stem: A brute-force checker handles a 30-project portfolio overnight. The portfolio grows to 32 projects. How many plans must it check now?

options.text: Twice as many, since the two new projects add one doubling
options.says: Each project doubles the count on its own, so two projects double it twice.

options.text: About 7% more, since the portfolio grew by about 7%
options.says: The count grows with 2 to the number of projects, not in proportion to it.

options.text: The same number, since a checker skips plans that break a rule
options.says: Brute force still enumerates every subset to find which ones break a rule.

options.text: Four times as many, since every added project doubles the plans

origin.section: Checking a Plan Is Cheap; Finding the Best One Is Not
